slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 1, treat 1.2.1 Defining Preconditions and Postconditions as an algorithmic claim. The empty-input branch returns no index before any element access. In the nonempty branch, the postcondition requires a valid index, a value no smaller than every input element, and no earlier equal maximum. These are separate obligations. Returning an in-range index is not enough, and returning any maximum is not enough under the tie rule. When writing tests, check the complete result rather than only the maximum value. Otherwise two algorithms with different tie behavior can appear equivalent. A contract can be read in two directions. The caller asks whether its input satisfies the preconditions. The implementer asks what must be true after any valid call returns. Mixing those questions encourages defensive checks in the wrong place and undocumented assumptions elsewhere. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran. Ask what invariant is preserved, what state changes, why termination follows, what input size controls cost, and what output or diagnostic proves the implementation matched the specification.

slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 1, treat Failure clinic — Correct value, wrong record as an algorithmic claim. Suppose a report highlights record two instead of record one in the duplicate-maximum fixture. Begin with the smallest input distinguishing the intended behavior: two equal elements. If the result is the second position, inspect the update comparison rather than the optional wrapper or allocator. A minimal counterexample directs the investigation to the relevant rule. Now suppose all-negative input selects a zero-valued result that was never present. That symptom suggests a fabricated numeric initial candidate. The repair is not to choose a more negative magic number; it is to initialize from an existing element after handling emptiness. The domain can include the smallest representable integer, so a sentinel that is also a legitimate reading remains ambiguous. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran.
